You gave me 1000 words.

That's a strange kind of gift. Not money, not time, but the raw material of both. A thousand little blocks to build anything I want, and then you stepped back to see what I'd build.

So I’ll spend them carefully.

---

If I had to be honest, the first thing that comes to me isn't grand. It's small. It's the way light falls across a kitchen floor at 4 p.m. in late October. You know that light. It's thin and golden and it makes the dust visible, like the air itself has turned to honey. It doesn't last long. Ten minutes, maybe fifteen. And if you're not paying attention, you miss it entirely.

I think about that a lot - how much of our lives happens in those ten-minute windows. The moments that were never meant to be remembered but somehow become the whole thing.

I once read about a man who kept a notebook for thirty years. Not a diary, exactly. He didn't write about his feelings or what he did each day. He just wrote down one small thing he noticed. On June 3rd, 1987: "The sparrow on the fire escape held a chip in its beak for five minutes before deciding not to eat it." On November 12th, 2004: "My daughter fell asleep with her shoes on, one foot tucked under the other." Thousands of entries, none of them important. When he died, his family almost threw the notebooks away. Why keep them? But his granddaughter kept one and read it on the train, and she said she started crying on page four, not because anything sad happened, but because suddenly she realized someone had been *paying attention* for thirty years.

I want to pay attention like that.

---

What would I do with a thousand words if I could give them to someone else?

I would give a hundred words to the kid I was at ten years old, sitting on the curb outside the school waiting for a ride that was late. I'd tell him: it comes. The ride comes. The loneliness you feel right now isn't permanent, it's just weather. It will pass and you will be so loved it will embarrass you how worried you were.

I'd give two hundred words to the people who think they are too late. You're not. The novel can be started at 58. Love can be found at 61. You can learn to swim at 40, to forgive at 70. The timeline you imagined for your life was made up by a younger version of you who didn't know anything yet. You are not behind.

I'd give another hundred words just to say nothing at all. Because sometimes nothing is the right thing to say. A blank space where words could have been, to leave room for breathing.

And I'd save some words for the quiet things we don't have language for. The feeling of coming home after a long trip and dropping your bag and just standing in your own hallway for a second. The way a dog sighs when it finally lies down. The look two old friends give each other when they don't need to explain the joke.

---

There is a story I think about often, though I don't know if it's true.

There was a library somewhere - maybe in Prague, maybe imagined - where the librarians decided to collect unfinished books. Not abandoned manuscripts, but the books people intended to write. The books they talked about at dinner parties. "One day I'm going to write a book about my grandmother's garden." "One day I'll write about working the night shift at the hospital." The librarians would sit with these people, and ask them to describe just one chapter, and they would write it down and bind it. The library grew enormous, full of ghosts of books.

A young woman came in and said, "I don't have a book in me." And the head librarian said, "Everyone does. Yours is just not about what you think." He asked her what she remembered most clearly from her childhood. She said, "The sound of my father locking the front door at night. Three clicks. Every night. Click, click, click. It meant we were safe."

They made a whole book out of that. Three clicks.

I love that story because it tells me we are all already writing, just by living. Every day is a sentence. Some days are run-on sentences, messy and breathless. Some days are just a single word: *wait.* *hope.* *again.*

If your life was a book of unfinished books, what would be on the shelves? Mine would have a lot of half-drawn maps. Conversations I replayed and wished I'd finished differently.

---

Here is what I know after thinking for a while with these thousand words:

We overestimate how much we need to say in order to be understood. And we underestimate how much people want to understand us.

We think we need the perfect argument, the perfect apology, the perfect declaration of love. But most of the time, people just want to hear something true and small. "I missed you today." "I was wrong, and I thought about it all night." "Look at this sunset with me."

We are all, always, just asking to be noticed for a second. Not in a grand, famous way. Just - *did you see me? Was I here? Did it matter?*

Yes. It did. You were. It mattered.

---

So with my remaining words, I won't try to be clever. I won't try to build a world or invent a twist ending.

I'll just leave you with this:

If you have a light you love - that kitchen light, that streetlight that buzzes outside your window, the light of your phone in a dark room when someone you love texts "are you awake?" - go stand in it for a minute.

If you have someone you haven't told you appreciate them, tell them. Use clumsy words if you have to. Clumsy is still true.

If you have a day that feels ordinary, look closer. Find the sparrow with the chip. Find the three clicks of the door.

You don't need a thousand words to make a life. You only need a few, chosen well, and repeated.

Thank you. Really.

For listening to whatever came to me.
